56.t: Wagon band battles and playing soft
56.s: Ory rode an automobile truck to catch other bands and played softly to draw crowds.
56.q: Oh. Huh? That was my main house. What happened? Tell them. Well, we were fighting until we wanted to get tired of bands. Tired looked like I always went out.

56.t: Tying wagons together and winning Joe Oliver
56.s: Black Benny tied wagons; Oliver was beaten and joined Ory, who corrected his tone.
56.q: Black Benning used to tie them with rope, you know. Oh, Black Benning. They wouldn't lock them, they'd lock them. They'd take a rope. Oh, rope. The other guy would try to get away from them and drag along with them. That's cool.

245.t: Advertising wagon battles with Punch Miller and Jack Carey
245.s: Bands bucked wagon to wagon on street corners; Durand with Frankie Dusen ran Punch off the corner.
245.q: Yeah. And you know like the band, the jazz band would meet on Sundays on advertising and buck against one another. Yeah. So I'd pull up there by Pete Lacoste and he'd be trembling, you know. Thought I was going to buck against him. I wouldn't buck. I'd just wave, you know, and go by. And me and…

567.t: The Onward band, white and colored bands, and band contests
567.s: White recalls colored musicians who played with the Onward band, string bands, and tying up wagons so a white band and a colored band could battle.
567.ch: Second lining and the brass bands
567.q: I forgot the Owenwood band, most of all them colored fellas was dead in the hornwoods. Oh yeah. Most of all them colored fellas was dead in the hornwoods. They had a few colored fellas in the hornwoods. Because plenty of times, plenty of times, plenty of times, plenty of times Manny Perez used to…

172.t: Wagon advertisements and battles between bands
172.s: Ridgley recalls advertising wagons where two or three bands met on corners and took turns, and players had to think up things to do.
172.q: It was a, sometimes you know, I don't know, you're just like anything else, you just, it's just off, it looks like you just can't get yourself together. Done the game, you're just to, let's get together and just tear them things open like that. The time they would get out on those wagon…

390.t: Kid Ory and advertising on the corner against rival bands
390.s: Desvigne worked alongside Kid Ory without being in his band, with competing bands advertising on the corner.
390.q: What did you remember? He played drums and trombone on them. Trombone, Celestine. Yeah, but he played drums, too, one time. That was Bebe Matthews. Bill Matthews, brother. Oh, yeah. Oh, Kid Ora, did you ever work with him? Oh, Kid Ora, I never did. I worked with him, you know, but I never was a…

256.t: Cutting contests with Buddy Petit and other Black bands
256.s: Wagon bands challenged each other; he did not hear Bunk Johnson or Oliver down there.
256.q: Then maybe an hour or so later we'd meet on another street, another corner.

184.t: Ory's swing beating other bands on the wagons
184.s: Hall recalls Ory's band in New Orleans winning street contests with a swinging rhythm, including a time with King Oliver.
184.ch: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
184.q: Oh, yeah. Because I thought he was the greatest drummer in the world. Yeah. Because one time, when we used to play on the wagons, you know what I mean? We met King Oliver once, and hooked up, you know, on the bands, hooked up down there. And I'll never forget, he was playing his number of Simmons…

259.t: Jack Carey advertising on the wagon and the Creole with the gun
259.s: Vincent tells how Jack Carey's band advertised dances from a wagon, a gun-carrying Creole stopped them, and he rode along as a boy of 13 or 14.
259.q: So did he play with Jesse Jackson? Yeah, he used to play with him. Right. He used to play with different bands too. He used to play with me, different bands. He'd go to Dave Parsons and grab the drum with a cab back. I had to go up there and get it. Uh, he used to call his son. But nobody know…

174.t: Bands advertising on trucks and competing on street corners
174.s: Bands advertised from furniture wagons and trucks, met on corners like a prize fight, with Chris Kelly, Punch and Kid Rena.
174.q: Yes, indeed. When Allen and them hit the street, when Ray Allen and them hit the street, I mean, Ray Allen and Guy Kelly, when he was playing with his dance band, Walter Pichon was playing mellow for him with them. When they hit the street, probably didn't roll up. I'm telling you.

568.t: The police ball and the 'cribs' repertoire
568.s: At the police ball he knew about five numbers, his 'cribs', tunes a band always had in reserve, and one won him $500 against Joe Oliver.
568.q: What do you mean? I never heard that term. That's numbers that we knew by head. All numbers, musicians used to play in those days. All bands had a crips. And no matter where he went to play, he'd never play that crips until they jammed him. Just like, we'll say Panama. Well that was our crips. See?…

264.t: Punch Miller, Jack Carey and advertising-truck bands
264.s: Photo of Punch at National Park; Zardis rates Punch below Rene and Chris Kelly and describes bands competing from advertising trucks.
264.ch: Other bands and the Philadelphia years
264.q: If I can find the picture. Yeah, well okay we can get it after. So Finney's telling you, well Punch was a terrible man with that, but Punch never could play like the rest of them guys, but he was good though. Punch was good. Yeah, Punch was a good man. Yeah, Punch was really good.

21.s: Rival wagon bands played against each other with applause deciding, and uptown favored Jack Carey while downtown favored Olympia.
21.ch: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
21.q: Oh, sure. Sure, we used to buck, we'd call that bucking. We'd say we'd stop this corner, and the fellow would say, Well, there's a kid right there at the next corner.

569.t: Bucking contests: Kid Ory against Jack Carey
569.s: He tells how Ory and Carey bucked each other with their bands on the wagons.
569.q: You'd call that bucking. Bucking. Yeah, yeah, you'd call that bucking. We'd run, there's Kid Oren them, oh, Kid Oren and Jack Carey used to buck all the time. They was known for that, those two, you know. They really used to pick on each other. Both played trombone, you know, and they both had…

570.t: Joining Buddy Petit and advertising on trucks
570.s: Playing with Buddy Petit at the fairgrounds and the Sunday advertising trucks where rival bands met in the street.
570.q: Well, when I started working with Buddy Petit, we used to play at the fairground here in New Orleans. That time, we used to have two bands there. I stayed with him quite a while. In fact, I was with him when he first took his stroke. First stroke he took. And we used to advertise in the streets and…

571.t: Band battles along the advertising route
571.s: Lewis explains how bands advertising a dance met on the street and played against each other, and how it was decided who won.
571.q: But I mean you'd pay an ad version. So you would start, like, down here and wind up, We have now, see. You'd come back down here, you're just bad. There's a different place, a different street where you know what people would do. There's a lot of streets. And the other time you met up with another…

572.t: Bucking contests between bands, and the Roger Wolfe band
572.s: Bands meeting on wagons would try to outdo each other with no declared winner; he likens it to a band he assembled against Roger Wolfe.
572.ch: Bucking contests, boogie woogie and rhythm
572.q: Oh, the bucking contest. Oh, well, well, well, that's all, all in that story. You didn't get a chance to read that thing about Smokey Mary.

127.t: Crowd words to Tiger Rag and bands meeting in the street
127.s: Audience sang 'Jack Carey on the water' during Tiger Rag; bands competed on street corners.
127.ch: New Orleans halls and street bands
127.q: Well, yeah, the people out in the audience started singing. When we were playing, when we got to that last spot, they said, Jack Carey on the water, selling pork chops, two for a quarter, you know. It just kept on going like that. They made a song, I assume. I couldn't remember it all. All I knew…

128.t: Punch Miller vs Kid Rena band contest on a Sunday
128.s: Jim recalls a street-corner contest between Punch's band and Kid Rena's, with Honky Tonk Town and blues, where cornetists were featured.
128.q: . . . . . . . It was 21, street they called Corner and Roman. It was like you said, two, that time they had wagons. It was Punch with his band and Kid Rene with his band, but he happened to have two corners. Rick, I was playing with him that Sunday. And the first number they played, I was just, I…

84.s: Handy recalls coming from Baton Rouge to play a contest against Celestin, won by Tup Johnson's band, and doubts it proved better.
84.ch: Reading bands and the jazz scene
84.q: Well, that's just like anything else. I don't know. They say Tup's won it, but I don't know. You take, uh, maybe that's because that was the first time they heard Tup's band. Everybody liked it. That didn't prove that they had a better band than Celestan. But, uh, first time hearing something, it…

573.t: Famous bands and advertising trucks and band contests
573.s: Oliver and Jack Carey bands were famous; bands on advertising trucks were challenged to out-play each other.
573.q: Ori had a good band and Jack Carey. Oh yes. Well them was famous bands, Jack Carey, and that's the time we was advertising then. On trucks for, for, for, for dancers, you see. Did your band play on those trucks at the L2, to advertise? Oh man, sure. T.L. gate, man, you hang, back up, like that call…

300.t: Bucking contests from the advertising truck
300.s: Playing from a truck to advertise a baseball game, Humphrey describes bucking rival bands with Lee Collins and Buddy Petit.
300.q: Yeah, Third and Willa, that's where the National Park was, Third and Willa. Well, the game was up at, uh, B-San Park. We was playing, the B-San Giants was playing coffee leads. Oh, man, the baseball players all on the back of the truck and everything, you know, sawdust and everything. We made it…

58.t: Sunday band battles on the streets of New Orleans
58.s: Punch recalls thirty bands on trucks, battles with Sam Morgan, and Buddy Petit's rich tone; winners were judged by hall attendance.
58.ch: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
58.q: Oh, it just like Buddy Petit playing. If he would have been a high note fellow boy, he'd have been a killer dealer. But his tone was so rich man. He had a bigger tone than Louis. Boy, there was some days though, brother. I don't see nothing here now like it. Well, Paul, every Sunday, them must have…

574.s: Kelly's band and Rene's met on Roman Street and neither would move for three hours.
574.q: I heard you used a mute and was good on the blues. Oh, on that Floyd's thing. The rubber plunger. Yeah. Oh I used to like him playing Kelly's Love. Song My hat over my arm and lay behind it. He was a good street man. In them days used to have some advertising. You get out on the street with a…
